From Energy Transition Pathways to Measurement
Requirements: A Scenario-Based Study of
Low-V oltage Grids
Nane Zimmermann1, Lukas Peter Wagner1,∗, Luca von R ¨onn1,
Florian Strobel2, Paul H ¨uttmann2, Felix Gehlhoff1,∗
1Institute of Automation Technology, Helmut Schmidt University, Hamburg, Germany
2PSI Software SE, Berlin, Germany
∗Correspondence: lukas.wagner@hsu.hamburg (L.P.W.),
felix.gehlhoff@hsu.hamburg (F.G.)
Abstract—Increasing penetration of electric vehicles, heat
pumps, and rooftop photovoltaics is creating thermal and voltage
stress in low-voltage distribution grids. This work links three
German energy transition pathways (2025–2045) with state
estimation performance requirements, evaluated on two SimBench
reference networks across three equipment quality levels (good,
medium, poor) and three VDE Forum Netztechnik/Netzbetrieb
(VDE FNN) measurement constellations that differ in the availabil-
ity of transformer and feeder-level instrumentation. Congestion is
caused exclusively by transformer overloading and voltage-band
violations. No individual line exceeds its thermal rating. Equipment
quality is the primary factor: under good equipment, congestion
remains nearly absent through 2045 (1/26 scenarios), under
medium equipment it emerges from 2035 (10/26), under poor
equipment from 2025 (25/26), reaching 208% peak transformer
loading. Without transformer instrumentation, voltage estimation
errors remain at 6–35% regardless of smart meter penetration.
Adding a single transformer measurement reduces errors by a
factor of 3 to 24, achieving median errors below 1.1% under poor
equipment. Per-feeder measurements achieve comparable accuracy
and outperform the transformer-only configuration under poor
equipment in rural networks (0.8% vs. 1.1%). In urban networks
under poor and medium equipment, transformer and feeder-
level instrumentation meet the VDE FNN voltage accuracy target
without requiring customer-side sensors. These findings motivate
prioritizing transformer instrumentation as an effective first step
for grid observability and supplementing the current consumption-
driven metering rollout with risk-based deployment criteria linked
to local congestion exposure.
Index Terms—low-voltage distribution grid, state estimation,
energy transition pathways, measurement penetration, distributed
energy resources, § 14a EnWG
I. INTRODUCTION
The transformation of energy systems toward climate neu-
trality is driven by the extensive electrification of end-use
sectors and the large-scale integration of distributed energy
resources ( DER s) such as rooftop photovoltaics, electric
vehicles ( EVs), and heat pumps [ 1]. Because these assets are

historically characterized by limited monitoring infrastructure
and a design centered on unidirectional power flows, their

larly relevant case study due to its advanced energy transition
strategy and its legally binding target of achieving climate
neutrality by 2045. The German regulatory framework § 14a
Energiewirtschaftsgesetz ( EnWG ) mandates a paradigm shift
fromgrid follows loadtoload follows grid, empowering
distribution system operators ( DSO s) to employ curative control
through the temporary curtailment of controllable local systems
during periods of acute congestion. While this regulatory
flexibility facilitates a more efficient utilization of existing grid
capacity compared to conservative static planning, it remains
strictly contingent upon meeting advanced requirements for
grid observability and state estimation ( SE) [3]. Consequently,
these developments make Germany a suitable environment for
analyzing the evolving operational and monitoring requirements
of increasingly decentralized and bidirectional distribution
networks.
Unlike transmission grids, LVdistribution networks were
originally designed for passive operation with unidirectional
power flows and limited simultaneity of high-power loads.
The increasing penetration of DER , combined with flexible
and electrified demand, leads to higher loading of lines
and transformers as well as voltage band violations [ 4,5].
Reinforcement of distribution infrastructure is capital-intensive
and slow, making operational congestion management and
improved monitoring essential in the medium term [2, 6].
Scenario-based studies frequently analyze alternative energy
transition pathways for DER expansion and quantify their
impact on congestion frequency, hosting capacity, or flexibility
requirements. However, many of these analyses implicitly
assume full observability of the network state [ 7,8]. In
practice, LVgrids suffer from sparse and heterogeneous mea-
surement coverage, asynchronous data streams, and incomplete
knowledge about topology and parameters [ 9]. This persistent
observability gap fundamentally limits the reliable detectionarXiv:2603.28945v1  [eess.SY]  30 Mar 2026

and, thus, assessment of emerging congestion situations.
As a key enabler of distribution grid monitoring, SE
has therefore gained increasing attention. LV SE approaches
typically combine transformer measurements, smart meter data,
and pseudo-measurements derived from advanced load profiling
of historical consumption data. Many implementations rely on
weighted least squares ( WLS )-based formulations. However,
the demand for higher observability in increasingly active
grids highlights the inherent challenges of LV SE [10–12].
While these methods can significantly improve situational
awareness, their accuracy strongly depends on the number
and placement of measurements, and the statistical properties
of pseudo-measurements [13].
At the same time, regulatory frameworks such as § 14a
EnWG in Germany introduce new requirements for grid-
oriented control of flexible loads via smart meter infrastructures
[14]. This regulation mandates agreements for the grid-oriented
control of devices such as heat pumps and EVcharging
points in exchange for reduced network charges. To ensure
non-discriminatory operation, it empowers DSO s to manage
these loads through economic incentives or direct power limits
while simultaneously requiring more precise digital monitoring
of the distribution network. These developments increase
both the availability of measurement data and the operational
need for reliable grid state assessment. In critical or non-
routine situations, insufficient data quality or uncertainty in the
estimated grid state may require manual intervention by DSO s
[15].
Despite substantial progress in both scenario-based grid
studies and LVSE research, the interaction between long-term
DER energy transition pathways, resulting congestion patterns,
and the measurement requirements for reliable congestion
detection remains insufficiently quantified. In particular, it is
unclear how measurement penetration levels must scale with
increasing electrification to ensure that congestion events can
be detected with sufficient accuracy and regulatory compliance.
This work addresses this gap by linking German energy
transition pathways for the period 2025–2045 with a systematic
evaluation of SEperformance under varying measurement
penetration levels. Three research questions structure the
investigation:
RQ1: Considering different grid equipment configurations,
in which energy transition pathways and at what
points in time do thermal and voltage limit vio-
lations emerge in LV distribution grids, how do
their frequency and severity evolve, and which grid
components are primarily affected?
RQ2: How does SEaccuracy and congestion detection
capability depend on measurement penetration, and
what minimum penetration levels are required to meet
established quality targets under pathway-specific
DER deployment?
RQ3: What regulatory adjustments to smart meter rollout
requirements and grid monitoring standards are nec-
essary to ensure adequate grid observability under theexpected DER deployment trajectories, specifically
in the context of § 14a EnWG?
To answer these questions, this work proposes a method-
ological framework that (i) derives congestion events and their
characteristics from scenario-based time-series simulations,
(ii) evaluates SEaccuracy and the detectability of thermal
and voltage limits as a function of measurement concepts,
and (iii) derives quantitative requirements for measurement
infrastructure and monitoring with direct implications for
current German regulations.
The main contributions of this work are:
1)A systematic coupling of three German energy transi-
tion pathways (2025–2045) to feeder-level time-series
simulations across three equipment quality levels, quan-
tifying the onset, frequency, and severity of transformer
overloading and voltage-band violations in representative
rural and urban LV reference networks.
2)An accuracy assessment of branch-current-based model
(BC-Mod )WLS SE under three VDE Forum Netztech-
nik/Netzbetrieb ( VDE FNN ) measurement constellations
and varying smart meter gateway ( SMGW ) penetration
across all equipment levels, showing that a single trans-
former measurement reduces voltage estimation errors
by a factor of 3 to 24 compared to smart-meter-only
configurations.
3)The finding that congestion in the evaluated radial LV
networks is caused exclusively by transformer overload-
ing and voltage-band violations, not by line overloading.
Under K2 and K1, transformer loading is directly
measured, making voltage estimation the operationally
relevant contribution of the SE. The VDE FNN voltage
target is met in urban networks under poor and medium
equipment without customer-side sensors.
4)Regulatory recommendations including prioritized trans-
former instrumentation, risk-based SMGW densification,
and extension of the VDE FNN quality framework to
cover the congestion mechanisms that actually occur in
radial LV networks.
The remainder of this work is structured as follows:
Section II reviews related work. Section III presents the
mathematical analysis of SE. Section IV analyzes the impacts of
energy transition pathways on load limits in LVgrids. Section V
addresses SEquality under varying measurement penetration.
Section VI discusses the results, derives regulatory implications,
and identifies limitations. Section VII summarizes the work
and outlines directions for future research.
II. RELATEDWORK
This work aims to quantify how the monitoring infrastructure
(measurement penetration and placement) must scale with
a strongly increasing penetration of electrified demand and
distributed generation in LVgrids to ensure reliable congestion
detection via SE. To position this contribution, prior work is
assessed against the following derived requirements (R):
1)R1: Pathway-to-feeder downscaling.The work must
translate macro-level technology scenarios (e.g., heat

pumps, EVs, rooftop photovoltaics ( PV)) into feeder-
level load and generation profiling, including spatial
uncertainty and simultaneity [16, 17].
2)R2: Physically grounded congestion characterization.
The work must quantify voltage-band violations and
thermal overloads using time-series or probabilistic grid
simulations, relating outcomes to the actual topology and
parameters of each feeder [17, 18].
3)R3: Operational consequences and flexibility.The
work must either (i) explicitly model active operation
(e.g., active network management, coordinated charging)
or (ii) clearly distinguish them from passivefit-and-forget
scenarios, i.e., scenarios that assume no curtailment or
flexibility activation to resolve constraints [19–21].
4)R4: Observability-aware monitoring. SEand monitor-
ing methods for LVgrids must cope with sparse, het-
erogeneous, and potentially asynchronous measurements,
including potential dependence on pseudo-measurements
[9, 22, 23].
5)R5: Measurement-to-detectability link.Beyond SEac-
curacy, the work must connect measurement penetration
(and sensor types) to thedetectabilityof operational limit
violations (congestion events) [23, 24].
6)R6: Benchmarking and reproducibility.Evaluation
must be grounded on reproducible benchmark grids and
time-series datasets (e.g., SimBench) to support system-
atic comparison of scenario results and SEperformance
[17, 25, 26].
The following subsections synthesize related work along
these requirements and derive the research gap.
A. Scenario Downscaling and Benchmarking
Luo et al. [ 27] propose an interpretable diffusion model to
generate long-term distribution load scenarios. Their method
integrates a transformer and temporal decomposition to cap-
ture multi-scale load patterns across seasons and years. The
generated scenarios achieve high fidelity in temporal and
frequency domains. However, the method operates on aggregate
system load data and does not explicitly translate macro-level
technology scenarios (heat pumps, EVs) to feeder profiles,
so (R1) is only partially met. It also does not simulate grid
constraints (R2) or incorporate passive operation, SE, or
reproducible benchmark grids (R3–R6). Fakhrooeian et al. [ 17]
systematically evaluate EVcharging and heat-pump impacts
on German LVgrids using 200 realistic feeder models. They
create scenarios of EVand heat pump penetration and run time-
series power flows. The study quantifies minimum voltages and
maximum transformer/line loadings for each scenario. Thus
it directly addresses (R1) by downscaling national EV/heat
pump adoption and using a physical congestion analysis (R2)
simultaneously [ 17]. For example, they observe voltage dips and
cable overloads at high heat pump penetration. They use real
feeder data (R6). They assume passive operation (R3) but do not
tackle SEor measurement issues (R4, R5). Overall, this paper
provides rich feeder-level scenarios with stress analysis (R1–R3,
R6), but leaves out monitoring and control aspects (R4, R5).Treutlein et al. [ 25] release the FeederBW dataset, containing
two years of measurements from 200 German LV feeders.
This dataset includes one-minute power flows, weather, and
detailed metadata (housing count, PV/EV/heat pump capacities).
By offering real-world feeder profiles under evolving DER
adoption, it fully supports (R6). It is intended for applications
like load forecasting, machine learning, and synthetic data
generation. However, as a data publication it does not perform
modeling or downscaling itself (R1–R5). One of its values
lies in enabling future researchers to generate realistic feeder
scenarios and test methods (R6). Meinecke et al. [ 26] introduce
SimBench, a benchmark suite of synthetic German power
systems. SimBench provides LV/medium voltage ( MV)/high
voltage ( HV) grid models and one-year time series of loads,
PV, and EVprofiles. The dataset explicitly aims to standardize
test cases for research. SimBench “simplifies reproducing
study results” by offering scenario data [ 26] fulfilling (R6).
SimBench’s future scenarios can serve as high-level inputs, but
the work itself does not generate downscaling or analyze grid
congestion (R1–R5).
B. Grid Congestion Analysis and Operational Flexibility
Damianakis et al. [ 19] provide a thorough review of LV-grid
impacts of PVs,EVs, and heat pumps. They summarize studies
showing that high DER s penetration can cause voltage rise
violations, phase unbalance, power losses, and overloading. The
review also highlights mitigation: violations can be significantly
reduced through coordinated voltage/reactive power control
and tap changer optimization, which adjusts the transformation
ratio to stabilize the grid voltage. This work addresses grid
effects (R2) and operational measures (R3), but as a survey it
does not perform new downscaling (R1) or involve SE (R4–R5).
Protopapadaki and Saelens [ 18] simulate multiple LV feeders
using stochastic building and load models to study PV and
heat pumps effects. They use a Monte Carlo simulation with
detailed, Modelica-based building models, which account for
the thermal behavior of the building envelope, its orientation,
and the window-to-wall ratio to capture realistic heat pump load
profiles. Their results show that air-source heat pumps impose
larger voltage drops and cable overloads than rooftop PV in
the studied feeders. They find rural feeders overload at heat
pump penetrations from 20% to 30%. This directly quantifies
congestion (R2). No active control (R3) or SE is included (R4–
R5). Delchambre et al. [ 20] present a probabilistic power-flow
analysis for a single LV feeder with battery assets. It covers
physical congestion due to random frequency containment
reserve and automatic frequency restoration reserve injections
(R2), and the operational impact of these frequency services
(R3). However, it has no scenario-downscaling (R1), no SE
(R4), and no detection strategy (R5), and it is not based on a
public benchmark (R6). Khan et al. [ 1] review optimization
and control methods for LVnetworks with high DER share.
They survey decentralized DER, demand response, and the
regulation of voltage levels through reactive power management,
typically provided by smart inverters. Notably, they summarize
quantitative effects of control: coordinated voltage control and

optimal tap settings can improve hosting capacity and reduce
constraint breaches by 20–67% [ 1]. This covers active methods
(R3) and indirectly less congestion (R2). However, it is a
literature review (no new data) and does not perform scenario
downscaling or SE (R1, R4, R5).
C. Observability and Detectability
Fotopoulou et al. [ 28] review SEalgorithms under sparse
measurements. They highlight that limited real-time data in
LVgrids negatively affects SEaccuracy and convergence.
This is tackled either with more instruments or with pseudo-
measurements [ 28]. The review covers various SEformulations
(WLS , Kalman) and the use of pseudo-measurements to
maintain observability. Thus it addresses observability (R4)
and partially discusses pseudo-measurements for unobserved
states (R5). It does not involve scenario downscaling or grid
simulation (R1–R3, R6). Mattoo et al. [ 29] present a modular
two-level Kalman filter state estimator for distribution grids
with asynchronous heterogeneous measurements. In Stage 1,
separate estimators process micro-phasor measurement units,
remote terminal units, and smart meter data. Stage 2 fuses these
into a global estimate. They explicitly handle different refresh
rates and latencies, enabling real-time SE with mixed sensors.
The measurements from these different devices are asyn-
chronous. This satisfies observability with sparse/heterogeneous
data (R4). It does not explicitly address violation detection
(R5) nor other requirements (R1–R3, R6). Paruta et al. [ 22]
design a greedy algorithm for meter placement on LVnetworks.
They use an enhanced DistFlow SEmodel (including cable
capacitances) to evaluate observability. Iteratively they place
one measurement device that improves SE accuracy the most,
until predefined SE error limits are met. On a 75-node Swiss
feeder, they achieve full observability with the minimum
number of required measurement devices. This work directly
addresses (R4) by improving SEobservability. It does not deal
with violation detection (R5) or other requirements (R1–R3,
R6). Buason et al. [ 23] formulate a bilevel optimization to place
a minimal number of voltage sensors and set alarm thresholds
so that any violation of voltage limits will be detected. The
upper-level minimizes sensor count and false alarms, while
the lower-level computes maximum voltages given uncertain
injections. They use linear power-flow approximations to
guarantee no violation escapes detection. Thus it explicitly
ensures detectability of limit violations (R5) and optimizes
sensor deployment (R4). Specific mentioning of operation type
(R3) and scenario downscaling (R1) are outside its scope.
Dehbozorgi et al. [ 24] develop a SE-based detection scheme
for false data injection attacks. They introduce cost functions
for misdetection and optimize alarm thresholds for each meter
using an autoencoder and largest normalized residual test. This
work shows how measurement placement and thresholding
affect detection costs. It relies on an SE(R4) and ensures
anomalies are caught under limited data (R5). Idlbi and Graeber
[30] propose a digital twin framework for LVdistribution
grids with high DER share, integrating SEwith congestion
management in a unified operational environment. The digitaltwin continuously estimates the grid state from heterogeneous
measurements and uses the estimated state to identify and
resolve thermal and voltage limit violations. It directly uses SE
under realistic measurement conditions (R4) and congestion
events are detected via estimated state (R5). Besides that,
congestion management is an explicit operational objective
(R3). The framework does not perform macro-level scenario
downscaling (R1), and no standardized benchmark grids are
used (R6). Koch et al. [ 31] evaluate the substitution of topology-
centred measurement infrastructure by smart meters for grid
state identification in six SimBench LVgrids, showing that
substitution becomes feasible at deployment rates between
30% and 60% when both voltage and current deviations
are considered. They further integrate this approach into
an agent-based local energy and flexibility market use case.
Asman et al. [ 32] extend this line of work by quantifying
expected deviations in grid state identification using a smart
grid interface module ( SGIM ) on the same six SimBench LV
grids. With SGIM measurements at all transformer distribution
lines, voltage deviations range from 0.27% to 0.58% and
current deviations from 1.69% to 9.19%. With only a single
measurement at the transformer supply line, the deviations
significantly exceed the 0.5% voltage accuracy target in five of
six grids, rendering the grid state identification unsuitable for
curative congestion management. These findings address grid
state identification with sparse measurements (R4) and current
deviations indicate limits of congestion detectability (R5), but
the analysis does not include scenario-based DER projections
(R1–R3) and uses SimBench grids (R6). V on der Heyden et
al. [33] address a complementary challenge by proposing a
privacy-preserving power flow analysis via secure multi-party
computation, enabling grid state identification without exposing
individual prosumer data. This work tackles the data privacy
constraints that limit measurement availability in practice (R4),
but does not address congestion detection (R5) or scenario-
based analysis (R1–R3, R6).
D. Summary of the Analysis of Related Work and Research
Gap
The systematic review of the literature, summarized in
Table I, reveals a significant fragmentation in current research
regarding the monitoring of LVgrids, consistent with the
broader literature gaps identified by [ 9]. While each requirement
(R1–R6) is addressed individually or in small clusters by exist-
ing works, no single study provides an integrated approach that
spans the entire chain from macro-level scenario downscaling
to observability-aware congestion detection.
The core research gap lies in the disconnect between long-
term grid planning and operational SE. While scenario-based
studies often provide detailed pathways for DER expansion,
they typically assume a ”perfectly observable” grid. Conversely,
SEresearch focuses on algorithmic accuracy but frequently
lacks the context of evolving congestion patterns resulting from
specific energy transition pathways. To bridge this gap, this
work proposes a methodological framework that links German
energy transition pathways for the period 2025–2045 with

establish a consistent reference framework for evaluating the

By utilizing reproducible benchmark grids (R6), this work
provides DSO s with quantitative guidelines for scaling their

III. MATHEMATICALANALYSIS OFSTATEESTIMATION
This section provides a mathematical perspective on LVgrid
SEwith a particular focus on the influence of measurement
infrastructure. In LVnetworks, limited sensor penetration, high
network complexity, and reliance on pseudo-measurements
significantly influence observability, accuracy, and operational
usability of the SE.
The following subsections analyze (i) the influence of
measurement penetration on mathematical observability and
practical detectability of critical grid states, (ii) suitable quality
metrics for assessing estimation performance, (iii) the resulting
requirements to the underlying platform architecture, including
data sources, preprocessing, and validation routines, and (iv) theBC-Mod branch-current WLS estimator used in the evaluation
of Section V.
A. Influence of Measurement Penetration and Pseudo-
Measurements on Estimation Accuracy
In the past, extensive monitoring of LVdistribution networks
was rarely required. Operational planning and grid security
were typically ensured through conservative design margins,
and critical events were mainly handled at higher voltage
levels. In contrast, LVgrids historically featured significantly
less measurement infrastructure than MV or HV systems.
At the same time, LVnetworks exhibit structural properties
that make SEparticularly challenging: they contain a compara-
tively much larger number of nodes and lines, and show strong
spatial load variability [28, 34, 35].
A critical prerequisite for applying WLS SE algorithms is
the so-called 2𝑛−1 criterion. For a system with 𝑛nodes, it
states that the number of independent measurements should

InHVgrids, the available measurement set usually exceeds

implementations. Pseudo-measurements are values that are
treated as if they are measurements but are not derived from
actual sensors.
Pseudo-measurements in LVgrids are often used to represent
active and reactive power injections, 𝑃and𝑄, at household
connection points. These values are usually derived from his-
torical measurements, aggregated load profiles, or standardized
consumption models. In the case of distributed generation,
feed-in may be approximated via reference plants or assumed
production patterns (e.g., PVprofiles). While such pseudo-
measurements enable the mathematical solvability of the SE
problem, they introduce considerable uncertainty and reduce
the estimator’s ability to detect localized issues [9, 34].
The accuracy and reliability of the estimated grid state
depend heavily on the available measurements. While a higher
number of sensors generally leads to higher accuracy, the
location, measured quantities, and measurement frequency are
important factors as well.
Whenever real measurement values are available, the accu-
racy of the estimated state improves significantly. In particular,
substation measurements (transformer secondary voltage and
feeder currents) and measurements at distribution cabinets
or switching points provide high informational value. They
constrain the network state at electrically critical locations and
reduce ambiguity in downstream branches. However, sensors
at individual household nodes such as smart meters, also serve
to increase potential SE if available.
As a rule of thumb, nodes and lines with higher power flows
or loads should be prioritized. If feasible, the remaining sensors
should be placed as far as possible from each other to increase
the variety of data available to the SE [9, 22, 23, 36].
B. Definition and Application of Suitable Quality Metrics

SEis not trivial. In contrast to transmission system SE, the
objective in LVgrids is typically not a perfectly accurate
reconstruction of the full system state, but rather the reliable
detection of operationally critical conditions such as overloads
and voltage limit violations.

provided by VDE FNN guidance on LVgrid SE[37,38]. In

validation. Since reference values such as 𝑉realand𝐼realare
typically unknown, tracking whether a target accuracy is
actually achieved is difficult. Direct error measures can only be
computed at locations where ground truth is available, which
is usually limited to a small number of sensor points.
A common practical approach is to use existing measure-
ments as reference values. This can be done by analyzing
the residual vector of the SE, which represents the difference
between the estimated grid state and the available measure-
ments. However, this representation is inherently biased, as
measurements are, by definition, available at these locations.
Consequently, residual-based evaluation is not representative
for non-measured assets [39].

Another approach consists of temporarily removing in-
dividual measurements from the SEinput and comparing
the resulting estimate with the actual measurement value.
This leave-one-out strategy provides additional insight into
local estimation accuracy in the absence of direct sensor
information. Nevertheless, it can only be applied at locations
where measurements exist and therefore does not resolve the
fundamental lack of reference values for the entire grid [40].
For a comprehensive evaluation of all grid nodes and
branches, alternative methods are required. Simulation-based
evaluation of SEperformance can provide deeper insights
into estimation accuracy. In this approach, representative load
and generation scenarios at different operating points are
simulated, resulting in a fully known reference grid state.
The measurement configuration available in the real grid
is then emulated and provided as input to the SE. The
estimated state can subsequently be compared to the complete
simulated ground truth. This method allows systematic testing
of different sensor configurations and operating scenarios.
However, it is not suitable for real-time assessment and requires
assumptions regarding load behavior, DER integration, and
network parameters [41].
For online accuracy assessment, uncertainty quantification
methods can be applied. In WLS SE , the uncertainty of
the estimated state can be approximated using uncertainty
quantification algorithms using the SEgain matrix. This
approach relies on assumed input uncertainties, typically
represented by the standard deviations of the measurements
and pseudo-measurements, and assumes Gaussian-distributed
errors. Consequently, the resulting uncertainty estimates depend
strongly on the correct specification of measurement variances.
In practice, these uncertainties are often not precisely known
and are approximated as constant values. Other online un-
certainty quantification methods are possible, but typically
suffer from similar limitations related to uncertainty modeling
assumptions [13, 42].
Beyond accuracy metrics, additional performance indicators
are important for practical deployment. These include conver-
gence behavior, runtime, scalability, and robustness against
bad data. In particular, robustness against measurement errors
and outliers is scenario-dependent and directly influences the
reliability of anomaly detection in real-world LVapplications.
C. Feedback with Platform Architecture: Requirements for
Data Sources, Filters, and Validation Routines
The achievable performance of LVgrid SEis not only
determined by the estimation algorithm itself, but also by
the surrounding platform architecture. In practice, SEis
embedded in a data pipeline consisting of heterogeneous data
sources, preprocessing routines, and validation logic. The
quality and consistency of these components directly determine
the reliability of the estimated grid state [14, 30].
A key requirement is the availability of a sufficiently high
number of measurement points. In general, higher measurement
penetration improves observability and reduces estimation
uncertainty. However, in LVnetworks the deployment ofsensors is often limited by technical constraints (e.g., communi-
cation availability, installation feasibility) as well as economic
considerations. Therefore, the sensor concept must be designed
carefully to maximize informational value per installed device.
Due to the limited measurement penetration, a robust pseudo-
measurement generation process is required. This includes the
derivation of active and reactive power injections from historical
data, standardized load profiles, or other statistical models.
The pseudo-measurement concept must be consistent with the
available sensor data and should be continuously checked for
plausibility.
Another critical aspect is the weighting of input data. In
WLS SE , measurement weights should reflect the actual
accuracy of the used sensors as well as the uncertainty of
pseudo-measurements. Therefore, knowledge about sensor
performance and pseudo-measurement generation quality is
essential. Incorrect weighting can lead to biased estimation
results, reduced robustness against bad data, and misleading
confidence indicators.
If a target accuracy must be met (e.g., for reliable detection of
overloads or voltage violations), this accuracy must be verified.
As discussed in Section III-B , methods, as well as underlying
data must be included in the platform.
Finally, the measurement frequency of all data sources must
match the computational cycle of the SE. If sensor updates
occur significantly slower than the SEcycle, the estimator may
operate on outdated information, which can reduce accuracy
and impair anomaly detection. Conversely, higher-frequency
measurements require appropriate data handling and filtering
to ensure stable and consistent estimator inputs [29].
D. The BC-Mod Branch-Current WLS Estimator
The SEimplementation evaluated in Section V is based on
the modified branch-current WLS estimator BC-Mod [13,43].
In contrast to the node-voltage WLS formulation, BC-Mod uses
complex branch currents as the state variables. This results in a
linear measurement Jacobian whose entries depend only on the
grid parameters, not on the current measurement set. Compared
to node-voltage SE,BC-Mod is therefore less sensitive to
measurement errors and pseudo-measurement inaccuracies, a
property that is particularly advantageous for LVgrids with
high pseudo-measurement shares.
The WLS state vector ˆxis constructed from the real and
imaginary parts of the complex branch currents for all 𝑀lines
across all three phases. The estimator minimizes the weighted
sum of squared measurement residuals:

Node voltages are not part of the state vector but are

The distinguishing feature of BC-Mod over the conventional
branch-current SE[43] is a backward sweep that incorporates
available node voltage measurements: each measured voltage
is back-propagated to infer a substation voltage estimate, and
the average of these estimates initializes the next forward

nonlinear SEformulations at significantly lower computational
cost.
The implementation also provides uncertainty quantification

the gain matrix G=(H⊤WH)−1, which equivalently serves

sweep equations using the branch impedances and the current
covariances. Both uncertainties are expressed as 95% credibility
intervals, supporting manual decision-making in non-routine
grid operation [15].

This section describes the methodological framework and
data scenarios required to compare various energy transition
pathways for Germany between 2025 and 2045. The primary
focus lies in benchmarking the targets established by the
German Federal Government against the projections of Agora
Energiewende and Fraunhofer ISE, particularly concerning
the expansion of charging infrastructure, electromobility, heat
pumps, and photovoltaics (Section IV-A ). Following the de-
scription of the simulation input data and the harmonization of
15-minute load profiles (Section IV-B ), the section outlines the
underlying methodology and modeling approach (Section IV-C ).
Finally, the results are subjected to a systematic evaluation
(Section IV-D).
A. Energy Transition Pathways
The following analysis compares three distinct energy tran-

The comparison focuses on (i) the number of publicly accessible
charging points, (ii) the stock of EVs, (iii) the number of heat
pumps, and (iv) the installed generation capacity of PVsystems

by the German Federal Government are benchmarked against

chargers. The majority (78%, 128,643 units) were normal
chargers. Total charging capacity amounted to 6.28 GW, with
the most common power class being 15–22 kW. In contrast,
in [54] 1,651,643 EVs are reported as of 01 January 2025,

2) Public Charging Points:The German expansion path

various model-based assessments suggest that a significantly
smaller network may be sufficient. Depending on the underlying
scenario, specifically regarding the share of private charging
and the speed of high-power charging (HPC) deployment,
projections for the same period range from 0.38 to 0.68 million
publicly accessible units. By 2035, even with increasing fleet
electrification, the estimated requirement remains in a corridor
between 0.58 and 1.1 million points, highlighting that the

solely on the number of units, current research emphasizes the

of these mid-term milestones is contingent on a synergetic

drivers include direct subsidies, market interventions to increase
drivetrain accessibility, and the anticipated 2035 mandate
for zero-emission new registrations. Furthermore, the rising
CO 2pricing serves as a cross-sectoral catalyst, systematically
increasing the cost-competitiveness of electric drivetrains over
internal combustion engines. The variance in 2030 projections,
ranging from 23.0 to 49.0 EVs per 100 HH in broader scenario
assessments, is primarily explained by the assumed degree
of socio-political stability and technological openness [ 50].
Scenarios assuming high degrees of transformation freedom and
early technological commitment result in the upper bounds of
these projections, while skepticism or political instability act as
primary constraints. Despite these mid-term uncertainties, long-
term projections for 2045 show a high degree of convergence.

of the passenger fleet, with projections reaching up to 48.5

This alignment suggests that while the trajectory’s velocity isdebated, the structural endpoint of the transition is consistently

expansion is characterized by a balanced growth paradigm
between rooftop and ground-mounted solar systems. For the
2030 horizon, statutory expansion targets and major energy
transition studies show a high degree of convergence, aiming
for a capacity of approximately 108 GW in the rooftop segment
[45,49]. This consensus reflects a policy design that seeks
to utilize existing built environments to minimize land-use
conflicts while decentralizing power generation. Variations
in alternative projections for the mid-term (2030–2040) are
primarily driven by three structural determinants rather than
mere institutional disagreement. First, supply chain resilience
acts as a critical variable. Scenarios assuming a continued
high dependency on non-European upstream markets project
a slower deployment rate due to potential logistical and
geopolitical constraints [ 50]. Second, the composition of the
system-wide renewable energy generation mix influences PV
scaling. Scenarios that prioritize an accelerated wind energy
expansion tend to require lower residual PVcapacities to
meet decarbonization targets, thereby reducing the modeled
pressure on rooftop deployment. Third, baseline calibration
accounts for some divergence, as projections that did not fully
incorporate the actual realized capacity of recent years tend
to underestimate short-term growth potentials [ 50]. In the
long-term perspective leading to 2045, the expansion logic
shifts toward amaximum-potentialapproach. Projections for
rooftop solar PVshow a massive scaling effect, with capacities
estimated between 246 GW and 337 GW [ 45,50]. The upper
bounds of these intervals are typically reached in scenarios
that assume an early recovery from supply chain constraints
and a strategic focus on high-density urban solar integration.
This substantial increase underscores the role of rooftop PVas
a primary flexibility provider in an electrified energy system,

regardless of the specific scenario-driven velocity of the initial
ramp-up.

heating sector is characterized by a strategic focus on the
rapid deployment of heat pump technology, though projections
regarding the long-term market penetration of heat pumps
diverge. Mid-term targets for 2030 range from 6.00 to 14.0 in-
stallations per 100 HH, reflecting a consensus on an immediate
technology ramp-up to displace fossil-fuel boilers [ 49,50,52].
The systematic variance in long-term trajectories toward 2045,
where projections vary between a doubling and a tripling of
the 2030 stock, is primarily explained by the modeled role of
alternative decarbonization vectors. In scenarios with a lower
heat pump density, a significant share of the heating load
is assumed to be met by the expansion of district heating
networks or the use of carbon-neutral alternatives such as
biomass and green-gas-ready boilers [ 49,50]. Conversely,
the most ambitious pathways (targeting up to 42.0 units per
100 HH by 2045) assume an almost exclusive electrification
of individual heating systems [ 52]. Beyond technological
substitution, the adoption rate is increasingly driven by shifting
economic framework conditions. The rising scarcity of emission
allowances within the EU ETS I framework acts as a cross-
scenario catalyst, as rising natural gas prices systematically
improve the cost-competitiveness of electric heating. This trend
is further susceptible to domestic fiscal policy. Specifically, the
reduction of network charges and electricity taxes is identified
as a critical lever to lower the operational costs of heat
pumps, thereby accelerating the transition away from internal
combustion heating [ 49]. Consequently, the divergence between
pathways is less a matter of technological feasibility and more
a reflection of the assumed intensity of carbon pricing and the
speed of thermal infrastructure integration.
B. Simulation Input Data
Building on the values reported in Table II, the missing
projections for public charging points, EVs, rooftop solar PV,
and heat pumps were first completed via linear interpolation
and extrapolation. For the year 2025, each of the three energy
transition pathways was anchored to the baseline scenario, i.e.,
the empirically observed value. Subsequently, existing load
profiles were compiled for public [ 58] and private charging
infrastructure [ 59], rooftop solar PVgeneration [ 60,61],
households [ 62], and heat pumps [ 63]. These load profiles
were harmonized to represent a full non-leap year (365 days)
at a 15 -minute temporal resolution. This results in 35,040
intervals, each associated with an average load in kW for the
respective 15-minute period.
For public charging points, in addition to standard weekday
and weekend profiles, outliers observed in the raw data
were explicitly modeled. The modeling utilizes load profiles
representing the 70th to 85th percentiles to reflect a robust
average demand. To capture potential peak-load events, a
specific high-power profile based on maximum observed
utilization was integrated for individual charging units across
all scenarios. Distinct load profiles for rural and urban areaswere available [ 58]. For private charging infrastructure, the
underlying load profile assumed a daily plug-in factor of 70%
with a charging demand of 3.68 kW (16 A, 230 V). Based
on empirical measurements, this implies that only 70% of
allEVs are charged on a given day [ 59]. For household
demand, the newly updated H25 standard load profile was
used. This profile reflects modern consumption patterns by
incorporating structural shifts in energy use over the past 25
years to provide a more precise baseline for current residual
demand. To adjust the reference single-family household profile
to seasonal variation, a dynamization function was applied
[62]. The original normalization to an annual consumption
of 1,000,000 kWh was rescaled to a baseline of 3,500 kWh
per household using a linear adjustment. This value represents
the upper range of average annual electricity consumption for
German households, ensuring a robust estimation of residential
demand [ 64]. The authors in [ 65] report that a multi-family
building in Germany comprises, on average, 6.76 apartments.
This value was rounded down to 6, and the single-family
household load profile was scaled by this factor to approximate
a multi-family building load profile.
For the PVgeneration profile, Germany’s average global
horizontal irradiation of 1,086 kWh/m² [ 66] motivated the selec-
tion of Frankfurt am Main as the reference location. Frankfurt
exhibits approximately 1,100 kWh/m², closely matching the
national average [ 67]. A typical PVsystem size of 11.5 kWp
was assumed [ 68]. Based on data from [ 69], the following
distribution of PVarray orientations was adopted: south (60%),
west (21%), and east (19%), resulting in a cumulative coverage
of 100% of the simulated capacity. To maintain this distribution
while accounting for all potential roof areas, north-facing
orientations were split evenly between west and east. To account
for regional differences in building stock, the heating demand
of urban heat pumps was assumed to be four times higher
than that of rural heat pumps. This scaling reflects the typical
difference in heating loads between multi-family buildings,
which dominate urban areas, and single-family houses, which
are predominant in rural contexts [70].
C. Methodology
The objective of this work step is to investigate when and
under which energy transition pathways grid congestions occur
inLVdistribution networks considering different levels of grid
equipment quality under the assumption of passive network
operation. The analysis focuses on the timing, frequency, and
severity of congestions resulting from increasing electrification
through public charging points, EVs, rooftop solar PVand
heat pumps. Methodologically, the study applies a time-
series power-flow analysis based on standardized SimBench
reference networks, scenario-specific equipment at NCP s, and
a formalized detection and classification of congestion events.
To establish a consistent reference framework, active
congestion-management measures are deliberately excluded.
In particular, storage systems, bidirectional charging, load
shifting, dynamic tariffs, and intelligent control strategies are
not considered. The analysis therefore represents a business-

as-usual case and quantifies when purely passive operation
reaches its limits in the investigated networks.
1) Selection and Modeling of Network Structures:The
study is based on standardized LV reference networks
from the SimBench dataset. To represent contrasting settle-
ment structures, two different networks are used. For the
simulation of urban scenarios, the open-access SimBench
code 1-LV-urban6--0-no_sw is used. It is character-
ized by densely built areas with predominantly multi-family
homes. The rural scenarios are based on the SimBench code
1-LV-rural3--0-no_sw which represents single-family
home areas with low connection density.
The network topology (lines, transformers, buses) and all
electrical parameters of the original SimBench data correspond
to thegoodequipment level described below and remain
unchanged for that level. All load and generation elements
originally contained in the reference networks are removed and
fully replaced by scenario-based load and generation data to
ensure that observed congestions result exclusively from the
defined scenarios. To limit numerical instabilities a minimum
line reactance of 𝑋min=0.001Ω is enforced. This value is
orders of magnitude smaller than realistic line reactances and
is only used to avoid extremely small or quasi-zero impedances
in the SimBench data without materially affecting the physical
relationships.

4) Congestion Events:A time step is classified as a
congestion period if at least one of the following conditions is
met: (i) thermal overload, i.e., loading of a line or transformer
exceeding 100%, (ii) voltage-band violation with 𝑈 <0.95 p.u.
or𝑈 >1.05 p.u., or (iii) non-convergence of the power-flow
calculation. For each congestion period, affected elements
(lines, transformers and buses) are recorded together with the
corresponding loading or voltage values.
To separately report near-limit operating states, agrey zone
is defined. Thegrey zoneincludes line and transformer loadings
between 100% and 110% and voltage deviations in the ranges
0.90–0.95 p.u. (undervoltage) and 1.05–1.10 p.u. (overvoltage).
Operating states outside these ranges are classified ashard
congestions, i.e., loadings above 110% or voltages 𝑉 <0.90 p.u.
or𝑉 >1.10p.u.
The root-cause classification for congestions is performed
per time step. If PVgeneration exceeds total demand in the
generation–load balance, the period is classified as generation-
dominant. Otherwise it is classified as load-dominant. Thermal
overloads are interpreted according to this dominance. Over-
loads under generation dominance are classified as generation-
side congestions, whereas overloads under load dominance
are classified as load-side congestions. V oltage violations are
assigned based on the direction of the deviation. An overvoltage
(𝑉max>1.05 p.u.) is interpreted as generation-side, and an
undervoltage ( 𝑉min<0.95 p.u.) as load-side. If both overvoltage
and undervoltage occur within the same period the time step
is labeled as a combined load-and-generation congestion. Non-
convergent periods are handled separately and reported asnot
converged, as affected elements cannot be uniquely identified
in these cases.5) Simulation Setup:For each of the 78 scenario–equipment
combinations (26 scenarios ×3 equipment quality levels), a
time-series simulation is performed over a full non-leap year
with 15-minute resolution (35,040 time steps). At each time step
all network elements are updated and a power-flow calculation
is executed using pandapower (Newton–Raphson, maximum
50 iterations). Non-convergent time steps are classified asnot
convergedcongestion events. No element-level overload data
are available for these cases.
Detailed element outputs are retained only for time steps
containing at least one congestion event. Key scenario-level
metrics, including congestion period counts, loading extremes,
temporal distributions, and element-wise overload shares, are
aggregated across all retained time steps.
6) Simulation Verification:A targeted validation study with
reduced problem size was conducted to confirm the correctness
of the simulation. One urban and one rural test network with
the same topology and number of NCP s as the main simulation
were used. Synthetic input data covering eight selected time
steps were constructed with known demand and generation
values to produce unambiguous expected system responses.
The eight time steps were designed to cover the following
conditions:
(1) Low loads and negligible PVgeneration: no congestion
expected.
(2) Household loads at daily peak: no congestion despite
elevated base demand.
(3) Very high PVinjection: generation-side overvoltage
congestion expected, validating PVorientation assignment and
generation-side classification.
(4) Very high private EV charging demand: load-side
congestion expected, validating per- NCP multi-device scaling.
(5) Very high public charging point demand: load-side
congestion expected.
(6) Very high heat-pump demand: load-side congestion
expected.
(7) Extreme simultaneous demand from all flexible load
types: solver non-convergence expected, validating the handling
of numerically infeasible operating points.
(8) Simultaneous high loads and very high PVinjection with
near-zero net balance. Individual households either exhibit both
very high load and very high generation simultaneously, or
have no demand or generation at all: no congestion expected,
validating the demand–generation balance logic.
For all eight time steps the simulation produced results con-
sistent with the expected outcomes, confirming the correctness
of scenario-to-network mapping, device penetration scaling,
congestion detection, and root-cause classification.
D. Grid-Side Congestion Under Passive Network Operation
This section analyzes the development of grid-side conges-
tion in urban and rural low-voltage networks under different
energy transition pathways up to 2045. It additionally analyses
the systematic variation of the grid equipment level, which is
shown to be the dominant factor governing congestion onset

and severity. Three equipment levels considered are shown in
Table III.
The focus is not only on the frequency and temporal
distribution of congestion events, but in particular on their
structural causes arising from the interaction between network
equipment quality, technology penetration, and the adopted
modeling assumption of purely passive network operation.
The objective is to derive systematic patterns from the
simulation results, such as equipment-dependent structural tip-
ping points into a persistently congestion-dominated operating
regime and the identification of particularly limiting network
components. Device penetration rates by scenario and year are
summarized in Table II (Section IV-A).
1) Development of Congestion Frequency:Figure 1 illus-
trates the development of the share of congestion periods in
urban and rural grids over the period 2025–2045, differentiated
by equipment level. A distinction is made between grey-zone
periods and hard congestion events.
The central result of Figure 1 is that the grid equipment
level is the dominant factor determining both the onset and
severity of congestion, with larger effect than the choice of
energy transition pathway. The three equipment levels produce
fundamentally different congestion regimes:
Undergoodequipment, the grid is nearly congestion-
free across the entire simulation horizon. Only 1 out of 26
simulated scenarios exhibits any congestion at all: the 2045
rural Fraunhofer case, which shows a marginal congestion share
of 0.03 % (12 periods out of 35,040), caused by a minor voltage
limit violation at a bus due to distributed generation. Maximum
transformer loading remains at approximately 80 %, well below
the thermal limit. This demonstrates that a well-dimensioned
grid can accommodate even the most ambitious electrification
trajectories through 2045 without requiring active congestion
management.
Undermediumequipment, congestion first emerges in the
urban network under the Fraunhofer pathway in 2035, with a
congestion share of 2.4 %. By 2045, urban congestion shares
escalate to 8.6 % under Federal Government conditions. The
rural network is first affected in 2045, where the Fraunhofer
pathway produces a congestion share of 1.5 %. In total, 10
out of 26 scenarios exhibit congestion. Maximum transformer
loading reaches 128 %, indicating that congestion, while non-
negligible, remains concentrated in a subset of high-stress
scenarios.
Underpoorequipment, the grid is already congestion-
affected in the 2025 baseline, with congestion shares of 1.6 % in
the rural and 2.7 % in the urban network. Congestion escalates
rapidly with increasing electrification: by 2045, rural congestion
shares reach 27–38 % and urban shares 31–37 % depending
on the pathway. Peak transformer loading reaches 208 % and
maximum line loading 98.6 %, indicating severely overloaded
infrastructure.
Across the different energy transition pathways, consistent
differences in magnitude are observable, but these are secondary
to the equipment effect. The Fraunhofer pathway shows the
highest congestion shares throughout, followed by the FederalGovernment targets and the Agora pathway. However, whereas
the choice of pathway modulates congestion severity within
an equipment class by a few percentage points, the transition
between equipment classes shifts the congestion onset by a
decade or more. This indicates that the structural capacity
reserve of the existing grid infrastructure, rather than the exact
expansion trajectory, is the system-determining factor.
2) Limit Violations at Network Components:Figure 2
quantifies which individual components exceed their operating
limits during congestion periods, showing the mean fraction of
each component type that is overloaded per congestion period.
Figure 2 reveals that the type and extent of component-level
violations depend critically on the equipment level. Across
all 78 scenario–equipment combinations, no individual line
exceeds its thermal rating (maximum observed line loading:
98.6 %, 2040 urban Fed. Gov. under poor equipment). Conges-

and, at higher stress levels, by voltage-band violations.
Undergoodequipment, no component class is overloaded
across the entire simulation horizon. Thus it is excluded from
Figure 1.
Undermediumequipment, the transformer emerges as
the dominant limiting component in those scenarios where
congestion occurs (from 2035 onward in urban grids, from

overloaded in nearly 100 % of cases. Node voltage violations
remain negligible in urban grids but reach approximately 15 %
of congestion periods in the rural 2045 scenario, indicating
the onset of a secondary voltage constraint under higher
electrification levels.
Underpoorequipment, two distinct violation regimes emerge
depending on the network type. Inurbangrids, the transformer

without meshed alternative flow paths. Under passive operation,

The pronounced seasonal and intraday structure of congestion
suggests that SE systems should be operated adaptively. During
time windows with elevated congestion probability, particularly
winter evening hours and periods of high PV feed-in in summer,
higher update rates and lower estimation uncertainties are
required. Grids with good equipment, in contrast, can be
monitored with lower temporal resolution.

under near-limit conditions and varying power flow directions.
Robustness under both high-load and high-feed-in situations
thus becomes a central quality criterion.
Because congestion occurs in structurally concentrated net-

nodes have a disproportionately large impact. Consequently, the
weighting strategy within the WLS framework should account
for the structural relevance of individual nodes rather than
applying uniform uncertainty assumptions.
Overall, the results indicate that a congestion-oriented SE
approach, prioritizing the transformer, main feeder sections, and
critical time windows while explicitly accounting for both load-
and feed-in-driven effects, is a key prerequisite for regulatory-
compliant and operationally reliable grid monitoring. The
equipment level provides a natural criterion for differentiating
SE design: grids with poor equipment require comprehensive,
high-resolution, and temporally adaptive monitoring from the
present, whereas well-equipped grids can be operated with
lower monitoring intensity until electrification reaches advanced
stages.
9) Structural Synthesis:The analysis shows that, under the
assumption of passive network operation, the grid equipment
level is the primary determinant of whether, when, and how
severely congestion occurs, with larger effect than the choice of
energy transition pathway. While well-equipped grids remain
largely congestion-free until 2045, the structural tipping point
is delayed under medium equipment and occurs already in the
baseline under poor equipment, where congestion reaches high
levels throughout the simulation horizon.
Energy transition pathways primarily modulate congestion
severity within a given equipment class but do not alter the
underlying congestion regime. The results further demonstrate
that congestion is driven by both load and feed-in effects:
winter evening peaks are dominated by demand from EVs
and heat pumps, while in later years additional feed-in-driven
stress emerges due to high PV penetration, particularly in
capacity-constrained grids. At the same time, PV generation
can significantly reduce congestion during midday hours in
high-demand scenarios by lowering net load, although this
mitigating effect does not offset simultaneity-driven evening
peaks.
Structurally, both urban and rural grids are primarily
transformer-limited, with congestion increasingly extending
into downstream feeder sections under poor equipment. This re-
sults in a transition from a predominantly vertical (transformer-
based) bottleneck to a combined vertical–horizontal congestionregime. The pronounced spatial and temporal concentration of
congestion has direct implications for measurement concepts
and SE design.
In particular, reliable grid operation requires a congestion-
oriented SE approach that prioritizes the transformer, critical
feeder sections, and relevant time windows, while explicitly
accounting for both load- and feed-in-driven effects. While
grids with good equipment can be monitored with reduced
intensity, poorly equipped grids require high-resolution and

A. Measurement Configurations and Input Data
1) Measurement Model and VDE FNN Constellations:
The SEinput is composed of two distinct data types: real
measurements and pseudo-measurements. Real measurements
represent values acquired by installed SMGW s, i.e., smart
meter gateways as defined under the German Metering Point
Operation Act (Messstellenbetriebsgesetz, MsbG [ 71]). Each
real measurement delivers the active and reactive power
injection at a NCP for the preceding 15-minute interval. These
measurements are modelled with a relative standard deviation
of𝜎real≈1.7% of the measured value [ 13], reflecting both
sensor inaccuracy and communication jitter.
The transformer secondary bus (slack bus) is always treated
as a reference node with a fixed voltage magnitude of 1.0p.u.
(b=231V per phase). This corresponds to the output voltage
regulated by the on-load tap changer ( OLTC ) of the transformer,
which maintains the LVbus at approximately 1.002p.u. under
standard operating conditions. The resulting approximation
error is below 0.2% and is accounted for in the slack voltage
standard deviation of𝜎 slack=0.5%.
The VDE FNN 2024 study [ 38] defines three measurement
constellations for LV SE , which differ in the availability of
additional grid-level metering beyond individual SMGW nodes:
•K1 – Feeder-level transformer measurement: Each out-
going feeder is individually metered at the transformer
secondary. Pseudo-measurements for non-metered nodes

are generated by distributing the feeder’s measured active
power proportionally to the nodes’ annual energy con-
sumption within that feeder. The VDE FNN recommends
a minimum SMGW penetration of 15 % for radial feeders
under this constellation.
•K2 – Transformer total power measurement: The total
active power at the transformer secondary is measured.
This aggregate value is distributed across all non-metered
nodes proportionally to their annual energy consumption to
form pseudo-measurements. The VDE FNN recommends
a minimum SMGW penetration of30 %.
•K3 – SMGW only (no transformer measurement): No
transformer or feeder measurements are available. Pseudo-
measurements for non-metered nodes are derived ex-
clusively from standard load profiles scaled by each
node’s annual energy consumption proxy. The VDE FNN
recommends a minimum SMGW penetration of 70 % for
this most conservative constellation.
This study evaluates all three constellations K3, K2, and
K1 across all three equipment quality levels. K3 represents
the baseline corresponding to the current rollout trajectory,
in which SMGW installation proceeds without accompanying
transformer instrumentation. K2 quantifies the benefit of adding
a single transformer power measurement. Feeder membership
is derived algorithmically from the SimBench LVnetwork
topology (breadth-first traversal from the transformer LVbus),
yielding 9 feeders (rural, 1–29 buses each) and 7 feeders (urban,
1–18 buses each).

Three SMGW placement strategies are evaluated to char-
acterize the sensitivity of SEaccuracy to how the available
sensor budget is distributed across the network. The power-first
strategy is an oracle benchmark: it sorts nodes by instantaneous
apparent power|𝑆𝑖|at each evaluated period and selects the top
𝑛realnodes. This power-first placement strategy is not intended
to represent an optimal sensor deployment. Instead, it serves
as a computationally efficient heuristic that prioritizes nodes
with high power flows, providing a consistent baseline for com-
parison without requiring additional optimization procedures.
Because this requires knowledge of actual loading at the time ofevaluation, it cannot be deployed in practice; rather, it represents
an upper bound on the accuracy achievable under ideal targeted
sensor placement. The consumption-first strategy sorts nodes
by annual energy consumption proxy 𝐸𝑎,𝑖(independent of
the current period), reflecting a DSO deployment based on
billing data rather than real-time loading and representing a
feasible, coordinated deployment strategy. The random strategy
selects nodes uniformly at random from all LV load buses as
a proxy for an uncoordinated rollout, with reported errors
averaged over ten independent realizations (seeds 0–9) to
reduce sampling variance. Power-first thus provides an upper
bound on achievable accuracy under ideal targeted deployment,
while consumption-first represents a practical lower bound
among coordinated strategies. The random strategy models
the expected accuracy of the current uncoordinated regulatory
rollout trajectory.
The reported accuracy metric throughout this section is
the mean normalized voltage error ¯𝜀(Equation 4, defined in
Section III-B ), averaged over the set Tof evaluated congestion
periods to ensure that reported penetration thresholds reflect
typical congestion conditions rather than any single extreme
snapshot.
To keep the evaluation computationally tractable, |T|=50
periods per scenario are drawn via stratified sampling over
two dimensions: congestion severity (four quartile bins by
maximum transformer loading) and congestion location (five
most-frequently bottlenecked lines plus a residual group).
Sample sizes are allocated proportionally to each stratum’s
share of the total period count, with periods drawn at evenly
spaced positions to provide implicit temporal diversity. For
the single good-equipment scenario (2045 rural Fraunhofer,
12 congestion periods total), all available periods are used.

4) Positioning Relative to State-of-the-Art Methods:The
results presented in Section V-C and Section V-D are grounded
in a specific algorithmic choice, the BC-Mod WLS estimator
on SimBench reference networks. This subsection situates those
results within the broader literature to clarify which findings
are specific to the chosen algorithm and which reflect structural
properties of LV SE under sparse metering.
Node-voltage-based SEformulations represent a fundamental
class of approaches in which bus voltage magnitudes and
angles are directly chosen as state variables. This formulation
enables a physically intuitive representation of the system
state, since once node voltages are known, all other electrical
quantities can be derived. However, the resulting measurement
functions are inherently nonlinear, requiring iterative solution
procedures based on repeated linearization of the measurement
model. Even in three-phase formulations, the Jacobian matrix
generally depends on the current state estimate and must
be updated iteratively, although approximations exploiting
distribution system characteristics can partially simplify this
structure [74, 75].
Across the literature, node-voltage-based and branch-current-
based estimators are reported to achieve comparable estima-
tion accuracy, while their main differences lie in numerical
properties, computational effort, and the handling of mea-
surement types. In distribution systems, practical challenges
such as limited real-time measurements, reliance on pseudo-
measurements derived from historical load data, and reduced
observability are consistently identified as dominant factors
influencing estimator performance [ 74]. In the context of this
work, these findings indicate that the observed estimation errors
under sparse metering are not primarily driven by the choice of
state representation, but are largely governed by fundamental
limitations of SE, in particular low observability and the
methodology used for the generation of pseudo-measurements,
including their associated uncertainty.
The BC-Mod WLS estimator evaluated here belongs to the
class of branch-current-based linear state estimators, which have
been shown to be well-suited to radial LVnetworks [ 43]. The
algorithm correctness verification in Section V-B confirms that
the implementation achieves sub- 0.001 % voltage error under
full measurement coverage, establishing a valid correctness
baseline. The mean errors observed under K3 at partial coverage(¯𝜀≈6 –35 % depending on equipment level and network type)
are consistent with the range reported for profile-based pseudo-
measurement approaches in the literature: Angioni et al. [73]
report mean errors of 10–30 % for H0-based estimators in radial
feeders at 15 % penetration, and Strobel et al. [13] show that the
WLS uncertainty bounds align with empirical error distributions
under similar conditions. K2 achieves ¯𝜀<2 % under poor and
medium equipment, outperforming all K3 configurations and
matching state-of-the-art results for estimators that assume
a measured transformer injection [ 34]. A recent systematic
review [ 9] identifies transformer-based anchoring as the single
most impactful instrumentation decision for LV SE accuracy,
consistent with the findings here.
VI. DISCUSSION
A. Synthesis of Results
The joint analysis of energy transition pathways (Section IV)
and SEquality (Section V) reveals that the observability
provided by the current regulatory minimum measurement
deployment is insufficient for reliable congestion management
under K3, the constellation corresponding to the current rollout
trajectory. Under K2 and K1, voltage monitoring is feasible in
urban networks but remains limited in rural networks.
On the congestion side, the simulation results show that LV
grid stress depends critically on both DER penetration and
the existing grid equipment quality. Under good equipment,
congestion is nearly absent through 2045 (1 out of 26
scenarios affected). Under medium equipment, congestion
onset shifts to 2035 in urban networks and 2045 in rural
networks (10 out of 26 scenarios). Under poor equipment,
congestion emerges as early as 2025, and 25 out of 26
scenarios exhibit congestion across the evaluation horizon,
with peak transformer loading reaching 208 %. Congestion is
caused exclusively by transformer overloading and voltage-band
violations. No individual line exceeds its thermal rating in any
evaluated scenario (maximum line loading: 98.6 %). In rural
networks under poor equipment, the initial congestion at 2025
is driven by generation-side overvoltage ( >1.05p.u. ) from PV
feed-in, while later congestion (2030 onward) shifts to load-
driven transformer overloading combined with undervoltage.
Equipment quality determineswhencongestion occurs. Under
K2 and K1, transformer overloading is detected directly through
the transformer measurement. The SEdetermines whether
additional voltage-band violations can be identified throughout
the network.
On the SEside, the findings reveal a consistent performance
hierarchy across the VDE FNN measurement constellations
K3, K2, and K1 that is robust across all three equipment quality
levels. Under K3 ( SMGW only), the mean voltage error at
Config-A remains between 5.7 % and 34.7 % depending on
network type and equipment level, and does not improve
with increasing SMGW penetration. K2 (transformer total
power measurement) reduces voltage errors substantially across
all equipment levels, achieving median errors of 0.5–4.9 %
(a reduction by a factor of 3 to 24 depending on network
type and equipment level). K1 (feeder-level measurement)

provides comparable voltage accuracy to K2 and outperforms
K2 under poor equipment in the rural network ( 0.8 % vs.1.1 % )
because higher loading makes feeder-level measurements more
informative. Urban networks consistently show lower SEerror
than rural networks due to the more compact topology.
Since congestion in the evaluated scenarios is driven by
transformer overloading and voltage-band violations rather than
line overloads, the operationally relevant contribution of the SE
under K2 and K1 is the estimation of bus voltages throughout
the network. Transformer loading is directly measured under K2
and K1 and does not require estimation. The voltage accuracy
metric𝑓𝑝99

VDE FNN target (≤2 % ) in urban networks under poor and
medium equipment ( 0.9–1.6 % ), indicating that the estimation
error is small enough relative to the 5 % distance between
nominal voltage and the 0.95p.u. violation threshold to support
voltage-band violation detection in these configurations. In
